public_comment.topic: A commissioner (addressed by the chair as "Keith," who had not yet spoken and seemed unfamiliar with process) raised concern that work at 390 Howard Street appeared to be altering the landscape/reducing wetland area with no erosion controls visible, and asked about using a drone to observe the property from the air.

minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held hearings on several wetland permit applications (10 Sandy Cove Road, 60 Cross Road, 417 Howard Street, 221 Electric Ave), approving or issuing negative determinations for most, and continued others (1083 Northfield Road, 390 Howard Street, 31 Round Road) due to missing materials or requested delays, at one point noting the commission was near losing quorum. The meeting also covered a Chapter 61 land-sale notification the commission voted not to pursue, a Mass Trails grant reimbursement update, trail-improvement and volunteer updates, and a lengthy, unresolved debate — led by Commissioner Peter Stella — over whether the commission's 30-foot "no-touch" wetland buffer bylaw is legally enforceable.

what_happened.line: The commission approved or issued negative determinations for wetland permits at several addresses, including Sandy Cove Road, Cross Road, Howard Street and Electric Ave.
A commissioner publicly questioned whether the commission's 30-foot no-touch wetland buffer rule has legal authority behind it, and the debate ended without resolution.
The commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a Chapter 61 land-sale notice for a West Townsend Road property.
Hearings for three properties were continued to June 18 for missing materials or applicant delay, and the board noted it was near losing quorum on one case.

why_it_matters: A homeowner or contractor working near a wetland relies on these permits and continuances to know what conditions apply and when a decision will come.
The unresolved question about the buffer rule's legal footing could affect how the 30-foot setback is enforced on any future project near a wetland.
Declining the Chapter 61 right of first refusal means the town will not pursue buying that land, leaving its future use to the private owner.
